## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.68573.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.68573.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

This manuscript is of broad interest to readers in the fields of RNA biology, epigenetics, and early development. The authors provide an exceptionally comprehensive description of the temporal dynamics of mobile element RNA, host defense protein, and epigenetic mark abundance across fruit fly early embryo development. Pairing this descriptive work with the first application of a rapid protein degradation system to maternal proteins in the model fruit fly embryo, the authors reject a previously accepted model that the maternally-deposited protein Piwi establishes gene silencing transmitted epigenetically to later stages of development.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Maternally inherited piRNAs silence transposons during Drosophila embryogenesis" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Kevin Struhl as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission. The three reviewers applauded this exceptionally comprehensive description of the temporal dynamics of transposable element RNA, of piRNA pathway proteins and of H3K9me3 across embryogenesis. The reviewers also agreed that the novel application of the auxin-degron system to maternally deposited proteins in the early embryo opens new avenues of research for the community. Finally, the inference that maternal Piwi may actually not set up epigenetic silencing in later life stages represents an important course correction for the field. You will see below, however, that the reviewers were unconvinced that the current data support the major claim of the paper articulated in title, abstract, and final model, namely, that maternal Piwi is required for transposon suppression. We welcome a revised version of the manuscript that stays closer to the data, guided by the list of essential revisions below.

Essential revisions:

New experiments/analyses

1) The reviewers were unconvinced that the data support the major claim of the paper- namely, that maternally-deposited Piwi silences roo. In wildtype embryos, the dramatic increase in roo by 4hr and especially the sharp increase between 2hr-4hr – compared to the comparatively subtle 2-fold increase upon Piwi degradation – makes careful developmental staging hugely important for inferences from the latter experimental data. An internal control to carefully calibrate the RNA-seq with progression of development is necessary. Moreover, the 297 transposon curiously shows just over 2-fold increase versus control. How can we reconcile this change with log10 mean expression is >3 on the Figure 5D but in Figure 1C, the 297 transposon RPMs are barely registering any RPMs throughout embryogenesis.

2) Related to point 1), the reviewers requested additional timepoints for the auxin-induced degradation experiment. Specifically, RNA-seq or even just qPCR well-after the timepoints reported for both roo and 297. These timeports are important for determining if these two elements still drop to original low levels by 12hr or 17hr despite Piwi degradation at the beginning of embryogenesis. If so, the major claim of the paper would be yet further undermined.

3) The reviewers appreciated the compelling loss of H3K9me3 across the genome and at roo insertions upon Piwi degradation. However, the reviewers were less convinced of the significance of H3K9me3 depletion for gene regulation. For example, in Figure 5-SuppFig-1D, the roo insertion with H3K9me3 is overlapping Hid promoter, it seems surprising that there is little change in Hid mRNA levels after auxin induced degradation and loss of H3K9me3 signal. Related, for Figure 3B, the authors should overlay their RNAseq data with the ChIP-seq tracks for lbm and Tsp42El (which are both normally expressed in the embryo). If the pattern is like what is shown on Flybase, lbm and Tsp42El expression may actually increase during embryogenesis in the same degree of H3K9me3 accumulation around the roo insertion. This pattern could oppose the model of direct or meaningful silencing by piRNAs. While there is clearly a piRNA-chromatin response at roo insertions, the effect on roo silencing may actually be quite modest, and the modesty of this effect may contribute to the perplexing lack of any later developmental phenotypes from the auxin-induced Piwi degradation.

4) The reviewers agreed that one of the most impactful contributions made by this report is the rejection of the model put forward by Gu and Elgin. To further probe what may account for the differences between the two studies, the authors could take advantage of their own data. Specifically, in Gu and Elgin, they found different TE families responded differently to the depletion of maternal Piwi – authors could pull these TE families from their genome-wide data to investigate the dynamics (expression and K9 enrichment in response to maternal piwi depletion), further addressing this discrepancy.

Language modification/softening claims/key clarifications

5) Even if the 2-fold increase in roo holds up after more rigorously controlled developmental staging, the reviewers remained unconvinced that such a subtle change (compared to the dramatic spike in roo expression WT embryos) warrants the current title (and the model in figure 5). Unless, for example, the 2-fold increase triggers additional roo transposition (as assayed by WGS), then the title/model appears overstated. Modification of this claim in the title, abstract, and discussion is required.

6) In the ovary, roo is the transposon family with the highest density of antisense piRNAs present and roo mRNA is strongly upregulated upon combined Aub/Ago3 knock-down (Senti et al., 2015). By contrast the authors state that roo is not regulated by the ovarian piRNA pathway (lines 760-763). Their statement, however, is based only on nxf2 KO flies, which inhibit specifically coTGS and not PTGS, in line with previous findings of roo being insensitive to Piwi-mediated regulation in the ovary (Théron, NAR 2018). A revision of this interpretation and referencing the papers showing potent piRNA-mediated regulation of ovarian roo transcripts by PTGS is necessary.

7) The authors' finding of 297 is interesting but needs more elaboration. Based on previous functional studies of piRNA coTGS mutants (e.g., piwi, mael, arx, mael), 297's response is categorized with TE families that are classified as "opposite categories" by authors' data and interpretation – 412 and mdg1 families. In these previous studies, similar to 412 and mdg1, 297 has burst transcription and reduced K9 in these mutants in ovarian somatic cells. I am puzzled by how to reconcile the authors' interpretation of Roo and 297 with these previous findings. Based on Figure1 – SfigF, the expression dynamics of 297 differs from that of roo. Can this be attributed to the absence of normalization by copy number?

8) Since roo is known to be potently regulated through PTGS in the ovary and Aub is maternally inherited, conclusions about somatic piRNA-mediated regulation of roo (and other PTGS-targeted transposons) requires depleting Aub in addition to Piwi. If this experiment is not feasible, a description of the limitations of Piwi depletion specifically regarding likely redundancy between embryonic coTGS and PTGS by Piwi- and Aub-piRNA complexes, respectively, is essential.

9) Images requires quantification. In Figure 2-supplement 1, for example, by only glancing at the images for piwi, panx, and nxf2 vs H2Av localization, I would not have drawn the same conclusion as the authors. Authors should quantify the co-localization of GFP and RFP foci to support their conclusion.

10) The reviewers found omissions in the methods section that require attention.

a. Given the challenges of diffusing small molecules across dechorionated embryos, additional detail about the development of the auxin systems is warranted.

b. Transposon-calling method in the w1118 genotype and the strain with the AID-tagged Piwi should be reported. In the auxin-degron study, the sequenced strain would be heterozygous, complicating TE calling with short reads. Might the uncertainty associated with calling TEs in heterozygotes have led to the confusing results in Figure 5D and E? (For Figure 5 – SFigure C-E, the H3K9me3 enrichment is not right at the boundary of 297 insertions, but a short distance from it). This is a sharp contrast to Figure 3A-B, which is more typical -are the 297 boundaries inappropriately shifted?

c. It appears that only euchromatic TEs were incorporated into the analysis – if so, please clearly state this.

d. The y-axes should be the same for Figure 2A (for piwi) and Figure 2-SFigE (for panx) and 2-SFigG (for Nxf2) to help with comparison across these factors. Same for Figure 2B and Figure 2-SF and H.

e. Details of the ChIP-seq analyses are missing. For some, the authors used rpm (e.g., Figure 3A) while at other places, authors used fold enrichment (e.g., Figure 5E-was the former not normalized to input while the latter was?)

11) What prompts the massive clearance of the H3K9me across the 177 roo insertions after 10h AEL and does this have a real link to Piwi/piRNA binding to the roo nascent transcripts? Maybe speculate on this more in the discussion?

12) Pg 9 Line 236 To determine whether roo might be competent for retrotransposition in embryos, the authors mined quantitative proteomic data for roo peptides of gag, pol and env, but this just establishes ORF expression, not the act of retrotransposition, which actually requires WGS analysis for new copies of roo TE insertions. I suggest changing to more accurate statement like "To determine whether roo mRNAs are effectively being translated during the pulse of embryonic expression, we mined quantitative proteomic data…"

13) What is the consequence of lower viability of dechorionated embryos in regard to RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses. When do the embryos die off and how would this affect the dynamic range of the analyses?

14) Calling the orientation of TEs from short read data is tricky. How were these data validated?

Reviewer #1:

This study provides the most solid characterization of Drosophila Piwi mRNA and protein levels throughout embryogenesis to date, with insightful data on Drosophila embryonic TE expression and H3K9m3 marks, and useful creation of a GFP-AID-Piwi fly strain that enables testing whether maternally contributed Piwi has a direct role in responding to TE expression and H3K9me3 levels in the embryos after auxin-induced Piwi degradation. I applaud the thorough analysis, well written prose, beautiful figures and movies, and well-designed experiments. All the data and reagents from this study need to be shared with the public in a revision of the manuscript that I would welcome to see.

But I have one major contention with the hard push of authors to fit the data to a desired hypothesis and mechanism which proposes that maternally-deposited Piwi/piRNAs have a direct role in "silencing" the roo transposon. This issue begins with the paper's title of "Maternally inherited piRNAs silence transposons during Drosophila embryogenesis". My critiques and interpretation of the data suggest to me that Maternal Piwi and piRNAs are 'Responding' to the major roo transposon expression burst during Drosophila embryogenesis, but the importance of a silencing role is debatable.Reviewer #2:

In this study, Fabry and co-authors combined elegant and novel genetic experiments, live imaging, and functional genomics to investigate the role of maternally deposit piRNA machinery, in particular piwi, in silencing transposable elements (TEs) in developing embryos. Surprisingly, they found that maternally deposited piwi, but not zygotically expressed piwi, plays a dominant role in silencing TE families that are predominantly active in the embryos, especially for Roo and 297. Their developmental time course analysis provides a detailed investigation for the sequential events during embryogenesis, namely the nuclear localization of piwi, the burst of TE transcription, and transcriptional silencing of TEs. While the authors' findings are exciting and seem well supported, there are some incongruencies with previous studies, and these need to be further addressed. This includes that piwi's role in maintaining, in addition to initiating, TE epigenetic silencing in somatic tissues and whether TE family 297's activities and host-directed silencing are predominantly embryonic. The varying dynamics among different TE families may worth further investigation (by performing analyses that are normalized by TE copy number) to gain a full picture of the role of piwi in suppressing not only Roo, but also other TE families. Some technical details also need further clarification. Overall, this is an important study that will further our understanding of how hosts suppress selfish genetic parasites.

Reviewer #3:

Argonaute proteins of the Piwi-clade are best known for their role in germline silencing of transposons, but both Piwi and Aub have been shown to also be highly expressed in somatic cells during early Drosophila embryogenesis raising the question of putative somatic regulatory functions. Fabry et al. address this important question by first performing a detailed characterization of endogenous expression of transposons and the transposon silencing piRNA pathway during Drosophila embryogenesis (Figures 1-3) and then an experimental test of the embryonic functions of maternally inherited Piwi/piRNA molecules using a new protocol for degron-mediated protein depletion in dechorionated embryos (Figures 4-5).

In the first part of the paper the authors describe strong embryonic expression of the roo transposon as well as embryonic expression of maternally inherited Piwi. Although this to a certain extent validates previous observations, the authors' comprehensive analyses of transposons and piRNA pathway genes in both transcriptome and proteome data adds a very valuable and novel overview of this gene regulation. In addition, the authors extend on the current knowledge in several places, for example by characterizing Piwi expression from maternal vs zygotic origin (Figure 2E-F).

In the second part of the paper the authors present an elegant implementation of auxin-mediated depletion of degron-tagged Piwi. By auxin administration to dechorionated embryos, the authors are able to deplete maternally inherited Piwi-piRNA protein complexes within 25 minutes. This is an important advance compared to previous RNAi-based methods. In the following analyses the authors describe Piwi-dependent embryonic heterochromatin formation at roo and 297 transposon insertions.

The experiments are in general well designed and controlled and the analyses are broad and comprehensive. As the authors highlight in the last paragraph of the paper, the presented data largely disproves the tested hypothesis of Piwi-piRNA-mediated somatic epigenetic gene regulation in the Drosophila embryo. This finding is important and will be of broad interest for the field.

My main reservation with the current manuscript is that I find the conclusions on embryonic transposon regulation to be unnecessarily overstated. I find that this overstatement somewhat overshadows the important findings that resolve the question of maternal Piwi-piRNA functions in embryo gene regulation.

A few hanging concerns remain that I trust can be quickly addressed. Note that the absence of tracked changes in the revision document made it difficult, at least in two instances, to track stated adjustments to the text. Please point to these changes with line numbers.

1. The referees requested that panel C from the figure for reviewers be included in the main text along with A and B (maybe as part of the supplement to figure 5? (rebuttal point 1)).

2. Please include language justifying the use of different approaches to analyzing the RNA-seq data presented in Figures 1C and 5D (rebuttal point 1).

3. Please add to the main text, possibly in the legend, that the different strains (w1118 and the degron strain) had different 297 insertion numbers/mean expression (rebuttal point 1).

4. Please point to where language referring to "further highlighted the different normalization strategies in…the text" (rebuttal point 1) is found.

5. Please point to where language referring to "Appropriate adjustments have been made to the text underlining the limitations of whole embryo approaches…" is found.

claims.claim: PICTS interfaces with general chromatin silencing factors including Su(var)205/HP1a, SETDB1/Eggless (Egg), and its co-factor Windei (Wde), Su(var)3–3/Lsd1, and its co-factor coRest, Mi-2, Rpd3, Ovaries absent, and Su(var)2–10.
claims.source: PICTS interfaces with general chromatin silencing factors including Su(var)205/HP1a, SETDB1/Eggless (Egg), and its co-factor Windei (Wde), Su(var)3–3/Lsd1, and its co-factor coRest, Mi-2, Rpd3, Ovaries absent, and Su(var)2–10 (Czech et al., 2013; Handler et al., 2013; Koch et al., 2009; Muerdter et al., 2013; Mugat et al., 2020; Ninova et al., 2020; Osumi et al., 2019; Rangan et al., 2011; Sienski et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Loci targeted by Piwi are decorated in repressive chromatin marks including trimethylated H3K9 (H3K9me3).
claims.source: While the detailed mechanisms of transcriptional silencing remain to be established, loci targeted by Piwi are decorated in repressive chromatin marks including trimethylated H3K9 (H3K9me3) (Klenov et al., 2014; Le Thomas et al., 2013; Rozhkov et al., 2013; Sienski et al., 2012; Wang and Elgin, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Loss of Piwi in Drosophila ovaries results in de-repression of TEs and correlates with a severe reduction in H3K9me3 deposition at their corresponding genomic loci.
claims.source: Loss of Piwi in Drosophila ovaries results in de-repression of TEs and correlates with a severe reduction in H3K9me3 deposition at their corresponding genomic loci.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior research.

claims.claim: Piwi and Aub, and to a lesser degree Ago3, have been detected as maternally deposited proteins in Drosophila embryos.
claims.source: Piwi and Aub, and to a lesser degree Ago3, have been detected as maternally deposited proteins in Drosophila embryos (Brennecke et al., 2007; Brennecke et al., 2008; Gunawardane et al., 2007; Mani et al., 2014; Megosh et al., 2006; Rouget et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Maternally inherited PIWI proteins have been observed in the pole plasm of syncytial embryos and in pole cells, the germ cell progenitors, after cellularization.
claims.source: Consistent with their adult roles, maternally inherited PIWI proteins have been observed in the pole plasm of syncytial embryos and in pole cells, the germ cell progenitors, after cellularization (Brennecke et al., 2008; Dufourt et al., 2017; Mani et al., 2014; Megosh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: During the early phases of embryogenesis Piwi is also present in somatic nuclei.
claims.source: Though, in adult flies, the piRNA pathway is restricted to the gonad, during the early phases of embryogenesis Piwi is also present in somatic nuclei (Brennecke et al., 2008; Mani et al., 2014; Megosh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Disrupting Piwi or other piRNA pathway factors in the female parent via mutation or RNAi leads to oogenesis defects and often results in sterility or patterning defects.
claims.source: However, probing piRNA pathway function during early embryogenesis has been hampered by a lack of suitable experimental approaches. Disrupting Piwi or other piRNA pathway factors in the female parent either via mutation or RNAi leads to oogenesis defects and often results in sterility or patterning defects that would confound the outcome of analyses (Cox et al., 1998; Czech et al., 2013; Handler et al., 2013; Khurana et al., 2010; Klattenhoff et al., 2007; Klenov et al., 2011; Li et al., 2009a; Malone et al., 2009; Mani et al., 2014; Muerdter et al., 2013; Pane et al., 2007; Park et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Transposon expression steadily increased following ZGA and peaked between 4 and 6 hr AEL.
claims.source: TE expression steadily increased following ZGA and peaked between 4 and 6 hr AEL (Figure 1B), similar to what was noted in prior reports (Batut et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: At the peak, transposon RNAs correspond to ~1.7% of the total embryonic transcriptome.
claims.source: At the peak, transposon RNAs correspond to ~1.7% of the total embryonic transcriptome, with levels at the later studied time points decreasing to below 1% of the overall transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The majority of transposon expression could be attributed to one single transposon family, roo.
claims.source: Interestingly, the majority of transposon expression could be attributed to one single transposon family, roo (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: At its peak at 4–6 hr AEL, reads derived from the roo TE accounted for more than 1% of the entire embryonic transcriptome.
claims.source: At its peak at 4–6 hr AEL, reads derived from the roo TE accounted for more than 1% of the entire embryonic transcriptome, corresponding to more than 70% of all TE-derived reads overall.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Reads derived from the roo TE at 4–6 hr AEL corresponded to more than 70% of all TE-derived reads overall.
claims.source: At its peak at 4–6 hr AEL, reads derived from the roo TE accounted for more than 1% of the entire embryonic transcriptome, corresponding to more than 70% of all TE-derived reads overall.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: roo transcripts were detected as early as stage 6 (in gastrulating embryos ~3 hr AEL) and localized predominantly to yolk cell nuclei.
claims.source: In agreement with our RNA-seq data, roo transcripts were detected as early as stage 6 (in gastrulating embryos ~3 hr AEL) and localized predominantly to yolk cell nuclei (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by RNA-FISH in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Stage 11 embryos (~5 hr AEL) showed strong roo RNA signal in somatic cells of the mesoderm.
claims.source: Stage 11 embryos (~5 hr AEL) showed strong roo RNA signal in somatic cells of the mesoderm, similar to earlier reports (Brönner et al., 1995; Ding and Lipshitz, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by RNA-FISH and supported by citations.

claims.claim: roo transcript levels were undetectable by FISH in late-stage embryos (>10 hr AEL).
claims.source: In contrast, roo transcript levels were undetectable by FISH in late-stage embryos (>10 hr AEL).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by RNA-FISH.

claims.claim: roo is an LTR retrotransposon.
claims.source: roo is an LTR retrotransposon and, as has been proposed for gypsy in ovarian follicle cells (Kim et al., 1994; Leblanc et al., 2000; Song et al., 1997), could potentially be packaged into virion-like particles, possibly enabling infection of germ cell precursors as a propagation mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about roo.

claims.claim: In transcriptionally silent embryos (0–2 hr AEL), over 6400 unique proteins were detected.
claims.source: In transcriptionally silent embryos (0–2 hr AEL), we detected over 6400 unique proteins.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: Compared to 0–2 hr embryos, the signal intensity of ~17% or 1114 proteins significantly increased (p<0.01) by over 25% in 5–7 hr AEL embryos.
claims.source: Compared to 0–2 hr embryos, the signal intensity of ~17% or 1114 proteins significantly increased (p<0.01) by over 25% in 5–7 hr AEL embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: 490 (or ~8% of) proteins significantly decreased (p<0.01) by over 25% in 5–7 hr AEL embryos compared to 0–2 hr embryos.
claims.source: We also detected 490 (or ~8% of) proteins that significantly decreased (p<0.01) by over 25% in 5–7 hr AEL embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: The majority of proteins (4652 or 72%) did not change by more than 25% between 0–2 hr and 5–7 hr AEL embryos.
claims.source: The majority of proteins (4652 or 72%), however, did not change by more than 25% between 0–2 hr and 5–7 hr AEL embryos.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: Compared to the early time point (0–2 hr AEL), 5–7 hr AEL embryos showed significant accumulation of roo peptides (p<0.01).
claims.source: Compared to the early time point (0–2 hr AEL), 5–7 hr AEL embryos showed significant accumulation of roo peptides (p<0.01) corresponding to its expression peak.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: roo encodes a single ORF (with a predicted protein weight of 272 kDa), which contains a group-specific antigen-like protein (gag), a reverse transcriptase (RT/pol), an envelope protein (env), two peptidases-like domains (Pep), and a zinc finger.
claims.source: roo encodes a single ORF (with a predicted protein weight of 272 kDa), which contains a group-specific antigen-like protein (gag), a reverse transcriptase (RT/pol), an envelope protein (env), two peptidases-like domains (Pep), and a zinc finger (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and protein domain prediction.

claims.claim: Peptides corresponding to the gag, pol, and env proteins of roo were detected.
claims.source: We detected peptides corresponding to the gag, pol, and env proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, bottom), indicating potential competence for retrotransposition.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: Detection of gag, pol, and env peptides from roo indicates potential competence for retrotransposition.
claims.source: We detected peptides corresponding to the gag, pol, and env proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, bottom), indicating potential competence for retrotransposition.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the detection of these specific peptides.

claims.claim: roo ORFs remained detectable at 10–12 hr AEL.
claims.source: Of note, roo ORFs remained detectable at 10–12 hr AEL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F), possibly suggesting substantial stability, as this was a time at which roo mRNA levels had diminished.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: With the exception of Piwi, genes involved in coTGS were both maternally deposited and zygotically expressed during the first ~10 hr of embryogenesis.
claims.source: With the exception of Piwi, genes involved in coTGS were both maternally deposited and zygotically expressed during the first ~10 hr of embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq and proteomic data.

claims.claim: Components of the PICTS complex, comprising Panx, Nxf2, Nxt1, and Ctp, showed abundant protein expression in the 5–7 hr and 10–12 hr AEL time intervals.
claims.source: Components of the PICTS complex, comprising Panx, Nxf2, Nxt1, and Ctp, showed abundant protein expression in the 5–7 hr and 10–12 hr AEL time intervals.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by quantitative mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: Piwi mRNA appears to be primarily maternally deposited, with zygotic transcript levels remaining low throughout embryogenesis.
claims.source: Of note, Piwi mRNA appears to be primarily maternally deposited, with zygotic transcript levels remaining low throughout embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, Figure 2A, B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Pre-blastoderm stage embryos (0.5 hr AEL) showed GFP-Piwi localized to the posterior pole where it formed a crescent-like structure.
claims.source: As previously reported (Brennecke et al., 2008; Mani et al., 2014; Megosh et al., 2006) and consistent with its maternal deposition, we detected GFP-Piwi during the pre-blastoderm stage (NC1–9, ~0–30 min AEL) localized to the posterior pole where it formed a crescent-like structure (Video 1, Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: As embryogenesis progressed and somatic nuclei migrated to the surface (NC 9–14, ~1.5–3 hr AEL), Piwi localized to somatic nuclei and to the pole plasm surrounding the nuclei of germline progenitor cells.
claims.source: As embryogenesis progressed and somatic nuclei migrated to the surface (NC 9–14, ~1.5–3 hr AEL), Piwi localized to somatic nuclei and to the pole plasm surrounding the nuclei of germline progenitor cells, as we and others reported earlier based on immunofluorescence staining of fixed embryos (Brennecke et al., 2008; Mani et al., 2014; Megosh et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Nuclear Piwi signal strongly decreased during mitotic cycles, with little fluorescence signal overlapping with H2Av-RFP during nuclear divisions.
claims.source: In agreement with an earlier report (Mani et al., 2014), our dynamic data revealed that nuclear Piwi signal strongly decreased during mitotic cycles, with little fluorescence signal overlapping with H2Av-RFP during nuclear divisions (Video 1, Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: Piwi was detected in somatic nuclei throughout the first 10 hr of embryogenesis; however, signal intensity decreased over time.
claims.source: We continued to detect Piwi expression in somatic nuclei throughout the first 10 hr of embryogenesis; however, signal intensity decreased over time.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: Similar to Piwi, both Nxf2 and Panx were detected in somatic and pole cell nuclei from the syncytial blastoderm stage.
claims.source: Similar to Piwi, both Nxf2 and Panx were detected in somatic and pole cell nuclei from the syncytial blastoderm stage (Videos 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: In contrast to Piwi, Panx and Nxf2 showed strong co-localization with H2Av-RFP during mitotic cycles.
claims.source: In contrast to Piwi, Panx and Nxf2 showed strong co-localization with H2Av-RFP during mitotic cycles (Videos 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting that while Piwi is predominantly excluded, Nxf2 and Panx are retained in the nucleoplasm during mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: While Piwi is predominantly excluded from nuclei during mitosis, Nxf2 and Panx are retained in the nucleoplasm during mitosis.
claims.source: In contrast to Piwi, Panx and Nxf2 showed strong co-localization with H2Av-RFP during mitotic cycles (Videos 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting that while Piwi is predominantly excluded, Nxf2 and Panx are retained in the nucleoplasm during mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data.

claims.claim: Embryos derived from females expressing GFP-Piwi showed strong maternal deposition of Piwi during early embryogenesis.
claims.source: Embryos derived from females expressing GFP-Piwi showed strong maternal deposition of Piwi during early embryogenesis (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1L), with GFP fluorescence in later stage (>12 hr AEL) embryos restricted to the germline cells.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by immunofluorescence.

claims.claim: Embryos derived from the reciprocal cross (control males x GFP-Piwi females) showed no GFP signal in the early embryos.
claims.source: Consistent with maternal deposition of Piwi, embryos derived from the reciprocal cross showed no GFP signal in the early embryos (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1M).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by immunofluorescence.

claims.claim: Zygotically transcribed Piwi is likely not relevant for coTGS until later in development.
claims.source: Strikingly, Piwi of zygotic origin localized exclusively to the cytoplasm of the germ cell progenitors and was not detected in nuclei, suggesting that zygotically transcribed Piwi is likely not relevant for coTGS until later in development.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that zygotic Piwi is cytoplasmic.

claims.claim: Piwi in both embryos and ovaries existed in complex with 23- to 28-nt piRNAs and showed nearly indistinguishable size profiles that were biased for antisense reads.
claims.source: Piwi in both tissues existed in complex with 23- to 28-nt piRNAs and showed nearly indistinguishable size profiles that were biased for antisense reads (Figure 2—figure supplement 1N, O).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by small RNA-seq.

claims.claim: Piwi in ovaries showed higher levels of antisense piRNAs targeting the TEs mdg1 and 412.
claims.source: Piwi in ovaries showed higher levels of antisense piRNAs targeting the TEs mdg1 and 412, in agreement with the majority of these small RNAs originating from the soma-specific flam piRNA cluster (Brennecke et al., 2007; Malone et al., 2009; Zanni et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by small RNA-seq and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Piwi in embryos showed high levels of antisense piRNAs targeting roo (~16% or all TE-targeting reads) and 297 (~9%).
claims.source: Piwi in embryos showed high levels of antisense piRNAs targeting roo (~16% or all TE-targeting reads) and 297 (~9%), consistent with an ability of maternally deposited Piwi to potentially recognize these TEs when expressed in the embryo.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by small RNA-seq.

claims.claim: Early embryos (0–2 hr AEL) showed low levels of H3K9me3 signal at 117 euchromatic, w1118-specific roo insertions.
claims.source: Early embryos (0–2 hr AEL) showed low levels of H3K9me3 signal at 117 euchromatic, w1118-specific roo insertions (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: As development progressed, H3K9me3 levels at roo insertions increased with a peak at 6–10 hr AEL.
claims.source: However, as development progressed, H3K9me3 levels increased with a peak at 6–10 hr AEL (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: Deposition of repressive chromatin marks correlated with the RNA expression of roo, yet the maximum of H3K9me3 accumulation lagged behind the RNA expression peak by approximately 2 hr.
claims.source: Thus, deposition of repressive chromatin marks correlated with the RNA expression of roo, yet the maximum of H3K9me3 accumulation lagged behind the RNA expression peak by approximately 2 hr.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: The deposition of repressive marks trailed the direction of transcription and showed higher signal enrichments in the regions downstream of the transposon insertions.
claims.source: Of note, the deposition of repressive marks trailed the direction of transcription and showed higher signal enrichments in the regions downstream of the transposon insertions, as previously observed for piRNA-dependent silencing in cell culture systems (Fabry et al., 2019; Sienski et al., 2015; Sienski et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in ChIP-seq data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 signal at euchromatic roo insertions of 16–18 hr AEL embryos showed diminished intensities compared to earlier time intervals.
claims.source: Interestingly, H3K9me3 signal at euchromatic roo insertions of 16–18 hr AEL embryos, which lacked maternal Piwi in somatic nuclei and no longer express roo, showed diminished intensities compared to earlier time intervals.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: Heads and ovaries showed no enrichment of H3K9me3 at euchromatic roo insertions, despite the presence of a functional piRNA pathway in ovaries.
claims.source: Similarly, heads and ovaries, both tissues from adult flies, showed no enrichment of H3K9me3 at euchromatic roo insertions, despite the presence of a functional piRNA pathway in ovaries.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: Maternal piRNAs program a response to a burst of roo expression during embryonic development but the deposition of H3K9me3 marks no longer occurs at developmental time points and in tissues where roo is not expressed.
claims.source: Considered together, these data suggest that maternal piRNAs program a response to a burst of roo expression during embryonic development but that the deposition of H3K9me3 marks, likely directed via coTGS, no longer occurs at developmental time points and in tissues where roo is not expressed.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Genomic loci in close proximity to euchromatic, w1118-specific 297 insertions (n = 20) showed dynamic deposition of H3K9me3 similar to roo.
claims.source: Genomic loci in close proximity to euchromatic, w1118-specific 297 insertions (n = 20) showed dynamic deposition of H3K9me3 similar to roo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: While H3K9me3 levels at roo insertions peaked between 6 and 10 hr AEL, 297 insertions showed the maximum H3K9me3 signal intensity between 2 and 8 hr AEL.
claims.source: However, while H3K9me3 levels at roo insertions peaked between 6 and 10 hr AEL, 297 insertions showed the maximum H3K9me3 signal intensity between 2 and 8 hr AEL, suggesting that these loci are targeted by coTGS earlier than roo insertions.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 occupancy at transposons such as mdg1 and 412 that were expressed during embryogenesis but lacked substantial maternal deposition of piRNAs retained low H3K9me3 levels throughout embryogenesis.
claims.source: In contrast, H3K9me3 occupancy at transposons such as mdg1 and 412 that were expressed during embryogenesis but lacked substantial maternal deposition of piRNAs retained low H3K9me3 levels throughout embryogenesis, though they showed a strong enrichment in ovaries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 signal at constitutive heterochromatin remained stable throughout the sampled time points.
claims.source: H3K9me3 signal at constitutive heterochromatin remained stable throughout the sampled time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), while H3K9me3 levels on chromosome 4 increased steadily throughout development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 levels on chromosome 4 increased steadily throughout development.
claims.source: H3K9me3 signal at constitutive heterochromatin remained stable throughout the sampled time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), while H3K9me3 levels on chromosome 4 increased steadily throughout development (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: Feeding flies for 24 hr with 5 mM auxin-containing yeast paste was sufficient to induce complete degradation of Piwi in ovaries.
claims.source: Feeding flies for 24 hr with 5 mM auxin-containing yeast paste was sufficient to induce complete degradation of Piwi in ovaries (Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and this depletion resulted in the de-repression of transposons (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by western blot and immunofluorescence.

claims.claim: Piwi depletion in ovaries resulted in the de-repression of transposons.
claims.source: Feeding flies for 24 hr with 5 mM auxin-containing yeast paste was sufficient to induce complete degradation of Piwi in ovaries (Figure 4B, C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and this depletion resulted in the de-repression of transposons (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by qRT-PCR.

claims.claim: Following a 1-day treatment, embryos laid by Piwi-depleted females developed without defects and showed similar hatching rates as their control treated siblings.
claims.source: Following a 1-day treatment, embryos laid by Piwi-depleted females developed without defects and showed similar hatching rates as their control treated siblings (Figure 4E, F).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by counting hatched embryos.

claims.claim: Longer auxin treatments resulted in more frequent deformation of embryos that was accompanied by reduced hatching rates.
claims.source: Longer auxin treatments resulted in more frequent deformation of embryos that was accompanied by reduced hatching rates (Figure 4E, F), likely due to patterning defects as a result of Piwi depletion from follicle cells.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by counting hatched embryos and observing embryo morphology.

claims.claim: In dechorionated embryos, a near complete degradation of Piwi protein was observed following 30 min auxin treatment of embryos collected for 0–30 min AEL.
claims.source: However, in dechorionated embryos we observed a near complete degradation of Piwi protein following 30 min auxin treatment of embryos collected for 0–30 min AEL (Figure 5A, B).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by western blot.

claims.claim: Early blastoderm embryos treated with 5 mM auxin showed rapid degradation of GFP-AID-Piwi signal, which was undetectable after 25 min of treatment.
claims.source: Early blastoderm embryos treated with 5 mM auxin showed rapid degradation of GFP-AID-Piwi signal, which was undetectable after 25 min of treatment (Figure 5C, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.

claims.claim: The removal of maternal Piwi in the early time window did not significantly affect the embryo hatching rate.
claims.source: Of note, the removal of maternal Piwi in this time window did not significantly affect the embryo hatching rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by counting hatched embryos.

claims.claim: The majority of transposons showed no significant expression change upon Piwi depletion; however, roo and 297 were significantly de-repressed (p<0.05) by more than twofold.
claims.source: The majority of transposons showed no significant expression change upon Piwi depletion; however, roo and 297 were significantly de-repressed (p<0.05) by more than twofold (Figure 5D), suggesting that Piwi impacts their expression during embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by RNA-seq and differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Piwi impacts roo and 297 expression during embryogenesis.
claims.source: The majority of transposons showed no significant expression change upon Piwi depletion; however, roo and 297 were significantly de-repressed (p<0.05) by more than twofold (Figure 5D), suggesting that Piwi impacts their expression during embryogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the de-repression observed upon Piwi depletion.

claims.claim: Piwi depletion severely impacted H3K9me3 signal over the transposon consensus sequence of roo and 297, but not that of other TEs.
claims.source: Piwi depletion severely impacted H3K9me3 signal over the transposon consensus sequence of roo and 297, but not that of other TEs (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq and differential enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: 154 bins with significantly reduced (p<0.05) H3K9me3 occupancy were identified, while only two bins showed an increase.
claims.source: We identified 154 bins with significantly reduced (p<0.05) H3K9me3 occupancy, while only two bins showed an increase.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq and differential enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Of the bins with lower H3K9me3 signal, 122 and 10 were within 5 kb of roo or 297 insertions, respectively.
claims.source: Of the bins with lower H3K9me3 signal, 122 and 10 were within 5 kb of roo or 297 insertions, respectively, thereby illustrating the impact of Piwi on chromatin states at genomic loci specifically targeted by maternal piRNAs.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq and differential enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: 205 and 63 individual euchromatic, degron strain-specific TE insertions of both roo and 297, respectively, showed a strong decrease of H3K9me3 levels in Piwi-depleted embryos.
claims.source: Furthermore, 205 and 63 individual euchromatic, degron strain-specific TE insertions of both roo and 297, respectively, showed a strong decrease of H3K9me3 levels in Piwi-depleted embryos (Figure 5F, G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F), while H3K9me3 levels at constitutive heterochromatin and on chromosome 4 were not affected (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 levels at constitutive heterochromatin and on chromosome 4 were not affected by Piwi depletion.
claims.source: Furthermore, 205 and 63 individual euchromatic, degron strain-specific TE insertions of both roo and 297, respectively, showed a strong decrease of H3K9me3 levels in Piwi-depleted embryos (Figure 5F, G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–F), while H3K9me3 levels at constitutive heterochromatin and on chromosome 4 were not affected (Figure 5H, I).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by ChIP-seq.

claims.claim: While roo and 297 TE levels were elevated upon auxin treatment in 2.5–3 hr AEL embryos, transposon expression returned to baseline levels comparable to untreated embryos in 6–7 hr and 7–8 hr AEL time intervals.
claims.source: Of note, while roo and 297 TE levels were elevated upon auxin treatment in 2.5–3 hr AEL embryos, transposon expression returned to baseline levels comparable to untreated embryos in 6–7 hr and 7–8 hr AEL time intervals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured by qRT-PCR.

claims.claim: The data strongly indicate a relationship between the deposition of repressive H3K9me3 chromatin marks at transposon insertions and maternally deposited Piwi-piRNA complexes.
claims.source: Taken together, these data strongly indicate a relationship between the deposition of repressive H3K9me3 chromatin marks at transposon insertions and maternally deposited Piwi-piRNA complexes (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combined RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing effects of Piwi depletion.

claims.claim: Maternal piRNAs are critical in the suppression of hybrid dysgenesis induced by paternal transmission of I- or P-elements in matings with females that lack these transposons.
claims.source: Indeed, maternal piRNAs are critical in the suppression of hybrid dysgenesis induced by paternal transmission of I- or P-elements in matings with females that lack these transposons (Brennecke et al., 2008; Khurana et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Epigenetic modifications induced by piRNAs appear to aid in piRNA cluster definition in the germline.
claims.source: Epigenetic modifications induced by piRNAs appear to aid in piRNA cluster definition in the germline (Akkouche et al., 2017).

results.result: Transposon expression, particularly of the roo element, shows a transient burst during early Drosophila embryogenesis. Transposon expression peaks at 4-6 hr AEL, reaching ~1.7% of the total transcriptome, with roo accounting for >1% and >70% of all TE-derived reads. RNA-FISH confirms roo transcripts are detected in somatic cells (yolk nuclei and mesoderm) from stage 6 (~3 hr AEL) to stage 11 (~5 hr AEL), but are undetectable in late-stage embryos (>10 hr AEL).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 are well-supported by RNA-seq data (C25-C29), RNA-FISH imaging (C30-C32), and are consistent with prior reports. The quantitative measurements are precise, the spatial localization is directly visualized, and the temporal dynamics are clearly documented across multiple time points with biological replicates.

results.result: Proteomic analysis reveals that roo encodes functional retrotransposition machinery that is expressed during embryogenesis. Mass spectrometry detected >6400 proteins in early embryos, with roo peptides (gag, pol, env) significantly accumulating at 5-7 hr AEL (p<0.01), indicating potential competence for retrotransposition. roo proteins remain detectable at 10-12 hr AEL despite diminished mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C42 are supported by quantitative TMT-MS data with statistical significance (p<0.01) and appropriate controls. The detection of gag, pol, and env peptides provides direct evidence for protein expression, though the inference of "potential competence for retrotransposition" (C41) is reasonable but not functionally validated.

results.result: Components of the piRNA-guided co-transcriptional gene silencing (coTGS) machinery show distinct expression patterns during embryogenesis. With the exception of Piwi, coTGS factors (PICTS complex components: Panx, Nxf2, Nxt1, Ctp) are both maternally deposited and zygotically expressed during the first ~10 hr of embryogenesis. Piwi mRNA is primarily maternally deposited with low zygotic transcript levels throughout embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by RNA-seq and proteomic data showing expression patterns across developmental time points. The distinction between maternal deposition and zygotic expression is clearly documented, with Piwi showing a unique pattern compared to other coTGS components.

results.result: Live imaging reveals dynamic localization patterns of Piwi and PICTS components during embryogenesis. Piwi localizes to the posterior pole in pre-blastoderm embryos, then to somatic and pole cell nuclei as development progresses, with signal intensity decreasing over time. Piwi is excluded from nuclei during mitosis, while Panx and Nxf2 are retained in the nucleoplasm during mitotic cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are well-supported by light-sheet fluorescence microscopy data with clear visualization of protein localization dynamics. The observations are consistent with prior reports (C46, C47, C48) and provide new insights into differential behavior during mitosis (C51, C52). The inference about retention/exclusion (C52) is directly supported by co-localization data.

results.result: Reciprocal cross experiments demonstrate that Piwi-piRNA complexes in embryos are exclusively of maternal origin. Embryos from GFP-Piwi females show strong maternal deposition, while reciprocal crosses show no early GFP signal. Zygotically expressed Piwi localizes exclusively to the cytoplasm of germ cell progenitors, suggesting it is not relevant for nuclear coTGS until later development. Only maternally deposited piRNAs engage Piwi in the embryonic soma.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C103 are strongly supported by reciprocal cross experiments with clear immunofluorescence data and small RNA-seq analysis. The experimental design directly tests maternal vs. zygotic contribution, and the cytoplasmic localization of zygotic Piwi (C55) provides compelling evidence for the inference that it is not relevant for early coTGS.

results.result: Small RNA profiling reveals that maternally deposited Piwi carries piRNAs targeting embryonically expressed transposons. Piwi in embryos and ovaries complexes with 23-28 nt piRNAs with similar size profiles biased for antisense reads. However, embryonic Piwi shows high levels of antisense piRNAs targeting roo (~16% of TE-targeting reads) and 297 (~9%), while ovarian Piwi shows higher levels targeting mdg1 and 412.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C104 are well-supported by small RNA-seq data from Piwi immunoprecipitations. The quantitative measurements are precise, and the differences between embryonic and ovarian piRNA populations are clearly documented. The data directly support the hypothesis that maternal piRNAs provide instructions for recognizing embryonically expressed elements.

results.result: H3K9me3 marks are dynamically deposited at roo insertions during embryogenesis in a pattern consistent with piRNA-guided heterochromatin formation. Early embryos (0-2 hr AEL) show low H3K9me3 at roo insertions, which increases to peak at 6-10 hr AEL, lagging ~2 hr behind the RNA expression peak. The marks trail transcription direction and are enriched downstream of insertions. H3K9me3 diminishes by 16-18 hr AEL and is absent in adult tissues despite functional piRNA pathway in ovaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are strongly supported by ChIP-seq data across multiple developmental time points with biological replicates. The temporal correlation with roo expression, the directional bias of H3K9me3 deposition, and the transient nature of the marks are all clearly documented. The inference that maternal piRNAs program this response (C65) is well-supported by the combined data.

results.result: The 297 transposon shows similar but temporally distinct H3K9me3 dynamics compared to roo. Euchromatic 297 insertions (n=20) show dynamic H3K9me3 deposition with maximum signal at 2-8 hr AEL, earlier than roo (6-10 hr AEL). In contrast, transposons lacking substantial maternal piRNAs (mdg1, 412) retain low H3K9me3 throughout embryogenesis despite being expressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by ChIP-seq data showing distinct temporal patterns for different transposon families. The correlation between maternal piRNA abundance and H3K9me3 deposition provides strong evidence for piRNA-dependent targeting. The negative control (mdg1, 412) strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: H3K9me3 dynamics at transposon insertions are specific and not due to global changes in heterochromatin. H3K9me3 signal at constitutive heterochromatin remains stable throughout embryogenesis, while chromosome 4 shows steadily increasing H3K9me3 levels, demonstrating that the transient dynamics at roo/297 insertions are locus-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are well-supported by ChIP-seq data providing important negative and positive controls. The stable heterochromatin and increasing chromosome 4 signals demonstrate that the observed dynamics at transposon insertions are not artifacts of global chromatin changes.

results.result: The auxin-inducible degron (AID) system enables controlled depletion of Piwi in ovaries. Feeding flies with 5 mM auxin for 24 hr induces complete Piwi degradation in ovaries, resulting in transposon de-repression. After 1-day treatment, embryos from Piwi-depleted females develop normally with similar hatching rates, but longer treatments cause embryo deformation and reduced hatching.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are well-supported by western blot, immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and hatching rate data. The system validation is thorough, demonstrating both protein depletion and functional consequences. The dose-response relationship (C73-C74) provides important context for interpreting embryonic experiments.

results.result: The AID system enables rapid depletion of maternal Piwi from early embryos. In dechorionated embryos, 30 min auxin treatment of 0-30 min AEL embryos causes near-complete Piwi degradation. Live imaging shows GFP-AID-Piwi signal becomes undetectable after 25 min of 5 mM auxin treatment. Removal of maternal Piwi in this early window does not significantly affect embryo hatching rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are strongly supported by western blot, live imaging, and hatching rate data. The rapid kinetics of depletion (within 25-30 min) and the lack of developmental defects (C77) are clearly documented, enabling functional studies of maternal Piwi without confounding oogenesis defects.

results.result: Depletion of maternal Piwi in early embryos causes specific de-repression of roo and 297 transposons. RNA-seq of 2.5-3 hr AEL embryos shows that while most transposons show no significant expression change upon Piwi depletion, roo and 297 are significantly de-repressed (p<0.05) by more than twofold, indicating that Piwi impacts their expression during embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are well-supported by RNA-seq data with appropriate statistical analysis (DESeq2, p<0.05) and biological replicates (n=3). The specificity of the effect (only roo and 297) and the control experiment without OsTIR1 strengthen the conclusion. However, the magnitude of de-repression is modest (twofold), which is acknowledged in the discussion.

results.result: Piwi depletion specifically reduces H3K9me3 at roo and 297 insertions without affecting global heterochromatin. ChIP-seq shows severe reduction in H3K9me3 over roo and 297 consensus sequences, with 154 genomic bins showing significantly reduced H3K9me3 (p<0.05), of which 122 and 10 are within 5 kb of roo or 297 insertions, respectively. Individual euchromatic insertions (205 roo, 63 297) show strong H3K9me3 decrease, while constitutive heterochromatin and chromosome 4 are unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are strongly supported by ChIP-seq data with appropriate statistical analysis and biological replicates (n=3). The specificity of the effect is demonstrated by both positive (roo/297) and negative (other TEs, heterochromatin, chr4) controls. The data directly link Piwi to H3K9me3 deposition at specific transposon insertions.

results.result: The effect of Piwi depletion on transposon expression is transient, but the relationship between Piwi and H3K9me3 deposition is clear. While roo and 297 levels are elevated at 2.5-3 hr AEL upon auxin treatment, expression returns to baseline by 6-7 hr AEL. The combined RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data strongly indicate a relationship between maternally deposited Piwi-piRNA complexes and repressive H3K9me3 chromatin marks at transposon insertions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by qRT-PCR time course data and the integrated analysis of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq experiments. The transient nature of the expression effect (C85) is clearly documented, and the overall conclusion (C86) is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence, though the modest magnitude of effects should be noted.

results.result: Piwi shows distinct localization dynamics during embryogenesis. Nuclear translocation of Piwi lags in germ cell precursor nuclei, correlating with delayed transcriptional activation compared to somatic nuclei. Dynamic imaging reveals that Piwi shuttles out of nuclei during mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by live imaging data and are consistent with prior observations (citations provided). The correlation with transcriptional timing (C92) is observational but well-documented. The mitotic exclusion (C93) is directly visualized.

results.result: roo is a highly successful transposon with unique expression patterns. It has the highest copy number in sequenced strains (9.4-9.9% of all TE insertions), shows extremely low expression in ovaries, and does not appear to be targeted by the ovarian piRNA pathway (no increase in expression or changes in HP1a/H3K9me3 in piRNA mutants). roo expression is activated by twist and snail in the embryonic mesoderm and expresses the full repertoire of proteins for virus-like particle formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are supported by whole-genome sequencing (C98), RNA-seq (C99), ChIP-seq and mutant analysis (C100), prior literature (C101), and proteomic data (C102). The convergence of evidence supports the hypothesis that roo has evolved a unique lifestyle, though the mechanistic details remain speculative.

results.result: H3K9me3 deposition at roo insertions is transient and correlates with the presence of piRNA pathway components. H3K9me3 marks build at euchromatic roo insertions as embryos progress to stage 13 (10 hr AEL), with the peak lagging ~2 hr behind transcription. By 13 hr AEL, H3K9me3 peaks disappear without roo expression returning, correlating with the absence of critical piRNA pathway proteins in the soma.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 are well-supported by integrated ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and proteomic data. The temporal dynamics are clearly documented, and the correlation with piRNA pathway protein presence (C108) is supported by the data, though causality is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Despite piRNA pathway targeting, roo remains highly expressed in control embryos. Zygotic depletion of maternal Piwi produces a statistically significant but modest change in roo expression (roughly twofold), yet roo remains highly expressed, reaching up to 1% of the entire transcriptome in control animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are directly supported by RNA-seq data. The modest effect size despite statistical significance is clearly documented and honestly reported. This observation raises important questions about the biological significance of piRNA-mediated control, which the authors discuss thoughtfully.

results.result: roo shows paradoxical features in ovaries: low expression without H3K9me3 marks despite abundant antisense piRNAs. Ovaries express roo at very low levels without H3K9me3 at euchromatic insertions, yet produce abundant roo piRNAs overwhelmingly in the antisense orientation. The uni-strand cluster 20A has collected roo insertions in the antisense orientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by RNA-seq, ChIP-seq, and small RNA-seq data from ovaries. The paradox of abundant piRNAs without silencing marks is clearly documented and represents an important observation about tissue-specific piRNA pathway function.

results.result: Recognition by the piRNA pathway does not necessarily create mitotically heritable epigenetic states. The transient nature of H3K9me3 marks at roo insertions demonstrates that piRNA pathway recognition does not impose mitotically heritable epigenetic states. This is consistent with observations in follicle cells where heterochromatin-mediated silencing requires continuous presence of piRNA machinery.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are well-supported by the temporal dynamics of H3K9me3 marks observed in this study and are consistent with extensive prior literature (multiple citations). The inference (C114) is strongly supported by the data showing loss of H3K9me3 marks when piRNA pathway components are absent, despite prior targeting.

results.result: Loss of transposon control in the embryonic soma does not cause overt morphological defects, but the piRNA pathway regulates somatic chromatin structure. Although Piwi depletion in early embryos does not result in overt morphological phenotypes, the ChIP-seq data showing H3K9me3 changes suggest the piRNA pathway plays a role in regulating somatic chromatin structure during early embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by hatching rate data (C116) and ChIP-seq data (C117). The lack of morphological phenotype is clearly documented, and the inference about chromatin regulation (C117) is well-supported by the H3K9me3 changes observed upon Piwi depletion, though the functional significance remains unclear.

results.result: Background knowledge claims about the piRNA pathway, transposable elements, and prior observations of maternal deposition. These claims establish the scientific context, including: piRNA pathway function in transposon control (C1, C13-C16), maternal inheritance of piRNAs (C2-C3), prior observations of maternal PIWI protein deposition (C21-C23), and various established functions of maternally inherited piRNAs (C87-C91).
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C11-C24, C87-C91, C94-C97) are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature and represent established knowledge in the field. They provide essential context for the current study but are not novel findings.

results.result: Summary of the study's main findings and hypothesis. These claims summarize the key observations (maternal Piwi in somatic nuclei, rapid depletion system, role in attenuating transposon expression, transient heterochromatin at roo) and propose a hypothesis that roo may have evolved to express in embryonic soma to evade germline silencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C9 accurately summarize findings that are supported by the detailed experimental data presented in the manuscript. Claim C10 is explicitly labeled as a hypothesis and represents reasonable speculation based on the observations, though it remains untested.

results.result: Structural characterization of the roo transposon. roo is an LTR retrotransposon encoding a single 272 kDa ORF containing gag, pol, env, two peptidase domains, and a zinc finger.
results.evaluation: Claims C33 and C39 are supported by established knowledge (C33) and sequence analysis with protein domain prediction (C39). These are straightforward structural characterizations.
